Hinged Tessellation 1

GeometryTrianglesConstructions
Game: This is a picture, not a game: squares and triangles fit together, and you can bend the squares into diamonds.
How to play: Drag A, B or C, or focus one and use the arrow keys. Change the rings and colours, then press Reset to start again.
Look for the math

This is a hinged version of a semi-regular tessellation. The middle square is free to flex into a diamond shape, but the triangles stay the same. Watch what happens to the corners when the diamond reaches 60 degrees. The live cut-the-knot page still embeds the original Java applet, so every rule, range and drawing step below comes from that applet's bytecode.

Five shapes at every corner

The starting pattern is written (4, 3, 3, 4, 3): walking around any corner you meet a square, two equilateral triangles, another square, and one more equilateral triangle. The numbers are the counts of sides, and their angles fill the whole turn: 90 + 60 + 60 + 90 + 60 = 360 degrees. That is what makes the pattern semi-regular: more than one kind of regular shape, but the same order at every corner. The logic test checks the four angles of the starting square and this sum exactly.

Something has to give

The page says there are two ways to put this pattern on hinges, because you cannot keep the squares and the triangles rigid at the same time. This first applet lets the squares go. A and C slide on the circle around B, while B slides on the line that cuts AC in half at right angles. Those restraints force AB = BC, and the fourth corner is D = C + A − B, so all four sides of the square stay equal: it becomes a rhombus. The other five points of each piece are found by rotations of 60 degrees and by the signed angle at C. The test follows A through every degree of the circle: the five triangles stay equilateral to within 10−7 of the drawing scale while the square's angles range from nearly 0 to nearly 180 degrees. Version B makes the opposite choice: it keeps the squares and frees the triangles, morphing toward a pattern of four squares at a corner.

Sixty degrees gives six triangles

When the angle at B reaches 60 degrees, the short diagonal AC is exactly as long as a side, so the rhombus splits into two equilateral triangles. Six triangles of 60 degrees then meet at each corner: 6 × 60 = 360 degrees, the (3, 3, 3, 3, 3, 3) pattern the page calls a derivative of the triangular tessellation. The same happens at 120 degrees using the other diagonal BD. The logic test checks both directions of the 60-degree drag: it measures the two halves, then walks the actual sectors around pattern corners and confirms six gaps of 60 degrees, not merely the arithmetic.

What the controls do

The page sets startLayer=4, and the applet's spinner runs from 0 to 15, so this drawing shows a centre piece plus four rings in each direction. Each copy is shifted by A − H along a row and by L − C between rows. The three radio buttons choose one colour, two alternating colours, or ten repeating colour bands. The logic test transcribes Stranger.Draw, Draw and ShowOneLayer a second time from the bytecode and compares every point, triangle, colour index and line over 36 positions of A, all three modes and layer counts 0 to 4, then over every spinner value through 15 and 24 positions of B. The dashed guide circle and line, the Reset button and the r shortcut are presentation aids; the applet had no such guides, and it had no win or loss.

Drag A until the status reports 60 degrees and watch the diamonds become two triangles each; then set Colour bands and slide the rings to 15.

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)
